newsitem.title: BOLIVIA: Bolivia's Banzer proposes revising privatizations.
newsitem.headline: Bolivia's Banzer proposes revising privatizations.

text.p: Gen. Hugo Banzer, who clinched the first round of voting and looks set to become the next president in August, says he will revise privatization contracts and seek to put an end to private monopolies.

In an weekend interview with Reuters, Banzer said that if he wins the second round in early August in Congress, he would try to convince foreign firms who invested in Bolivia's privatization to either scrap or cut short the seven-year monopoly many have been granted.

Moreover, several privatization contracts negotiated by President Gonzalo Sanchez de Lozada's outgoing administration were never made public, lacking transparency and making supervision difficult, he said.
"Some contracts are a mystery," he stresed.

As an example, he cited the sale of half the shares of the railways system to Chilean firm Cruz Blanca for $13 million, when the stock had a book value of $29 million. That was expressly barred by law. "Cruz Blanca will have to explain that," he said.

But the 71-year-old general made clear he would not try to coerce firms into accepting the new terms. "We will do it through dialogue," he said. He pointed out that "revising" was not the same as "reverting".

He will also try to convince foreign firms, especially in the oil sector, to increase their investments way beyond what has agreed in the contracts to help spur economic growth in Bolivia, one of the poorest nations in Latin America.
"I would say we need to dig 200 wells a year, not eight. Otherwise, we will never get a jump start," he stressed.
Dutch-Shell, Amoco, and Argentinas's YPF and Perez Companc have invested in Bolivia's oil sector since Sanchez de Lozada launched an ambitious privatization program.
Banzer said that while he fully supported the country's free-market drive launched 12 years ago, under Sanchez de Lozada the rich were getting richer and the poor poorer.
"Wealth has been concentrated on the top of the social pyramid," he complained. About 70 percent of Bolivians live under the poverty line. "This (economic) model has been dehumanized."
Banzer plans to continue in the market path which his Democratic Nationalist Alliance (ADN) party helped launch in 1985, but says he will seek to do it with a higher degree of citizen participation.

"The people are scared because there is no dialogue. Not a single day goes by without a strike, a stoppage, a road blockade," he said referring to widespread labor action against the government's economic policies.
By opening up the economy to foreign investment and high technology, the Sanchez de Lozada administration also threw thousands of people out of their jobs, he said.
The general said he would implement a system of micro loans to help 1.9 million people who have no steady source of income set up their own business or shop.

"Those are able people. Some are good working with wood, others may make good mechanics, others have an ability to work in electricity, sewing or knitting. They just don't use their abilities because they lack a launching pad," he said.
